title: Relational Databases (Basic): Azure SQL
reading:
Today's menu

By the end of this lunch you will be able to:

- Choose a database service for a workload by comparing Azure SQL Database, Azure SQL Managed Instance, SQL Server on Azure VMs, Azure Database for PostgreSQL and MySQL, and Azure Cosmos DB.
- Explain what an Azure SQL logical server is and how databases and elastic pools relate to it.
- Compare the DTU and vCore purchasing models, the vCore service tiers, serverless compute and the free offer.
- Describe how a connection reaches a database — gateway, firewall, Microsoft Entra authentication — and why Entra-only authentication is the safer default.

Meanwhile at Nusantara Retail

Last lunch, Dewi moved the storefront code to App Service. The orders, however, still live in a SQL Server Express database on the server next to the pantry. The only backup is a USB drive that Pak Budi takes home on Fridays, and last week that drive turned out to hold a copy that was three weeks old. Ibu Sari has stopped smiling about it.

Everyone has an opinion. Dewi wants a managed database she never has to patch. Pak Budi worries about who can reach it: today anyone on the office Wi-Fi who knows the shared sa password can. Rizky, the contractor, suggests "just opening port 1433 to the internet" so his reporting tool can connect from anywhere. The finance team only asks what it will cost.

Your job today is to pick the right database service for the orders, connect to it with your own identity instead of a shared password, and keep its door closed to everyone else. Which Azure database should hold Nusantara Retail's orders — and who should be allowed through the door?

Reading

1. Relational or not? Choosing a database on Azure

Every order on the storefront turns into a handful of rows: one row in an Orders table, a few rows in an OrderLines table, and links to rows in Customers and Products. That is relational data: information kept in tables with a fixed set of columns (the schema), connected by keys, and changed by transactions that either finish completely or not at all. When a customer pays, the order, its lines and the stock update must succeed together. That all-or-nothing promise is usually summarised as ACID (atomic, consistent, isolated, durable). You read and change relational data with SQL; Microsoft's dialect of it is called T-SQL.

Non-relational (or NoSQL) databases relax some of those rules in exchange for flexibility and scale. They store documents whose shape can differ from item to item, key-value pairs, graphs or wide column families. A product catalogue where a batik shirt has fabric and motif attributes but a rice cooker has wattage and capacity fits a document model nicely. You will meet Azure Cosmos DB, Azure's NoSQL service, in the next lunch.

Azure offers several managed homes for relational data, plus Cosmos DB for everything else. Keep this database choice matrix handy; it answers most "which database should we use?" conversations.

Service | Model | Engine | Pick it when | Think twice when
Azure SQL Database | PaaS | SQL Server engine, always the latest version | you build or modernise an app that speaks T-SQL and want Microsoft to handle patching, backups and high availability | you need instance-level features such as SQL Server Agent jobs or queries across databases
Azure SQL Managed Instance | PaaS, inside your virtual network | SQL Server engine with near-100% compatibility | you lift and shift an existing SQL Server application that depends on instance features | you only need one simple database — it costs more and takes longer to deploy
SQL Server on Azure VMs | IaaS | any SQL Server version and edition you install | you need the operating system, an older SQL Server version, or other software on the same machine | you do not want to patch, back up and cluster it yourself
Azure Database for PostgreSQL – flexible server | PaaS | community PostgreSQL | your app and team already use PostgreSQL and its extensions | your code is written in T-SQL
Azure Database for MySQL – flexible server | PaaS | community MySQL | you run PHP or LAMP-stack apps such as WordPress | you need SQL Server features
Azure Cosmos DB | PaaS, globally distributed | NoSQL, several APIs | flexible schemas, massive scale, fast reads close to users worldwide | you need joins across many tables and complex multi-row transactions

The older single server deployment option for PostgreSQL and MySQL has been retired (MySQL in September 2024, PostgreSQL in March 2025). Flexible server is the option to use for both today.

Using more than one database is normal. Many companies keep orders and payments in a relational database and put a catalogue, shopping carts or telemetry in a NoSQL store. The skill is matching each kind of data to the service that suits it, rather than forcing everything into whichever database you already know.

Read the decision flow below from the top. It asks about the data first, then the engine, then how much control you need. Each step towards IaaS gives you more control, and more work — exactly the shared-responsibility trade-off from Lunch 02.

2. The Azure SQL family and the logical server

Azure SQL is the umbrella name for three ways to run the SQL Server engine in Azure. They share the same engine, so your T-SQL skills, drivers and tools carry over. What changes is who does the operational work.

Deployment option | What you get | You manage | Pick it for
SQL Database — single database | one fully managed database with its own guaranteed resources | schema, data and access | most new applications
SQL Database — elastic pool | many databases sharing one pool of resources | the same, plus the pool size | groups of databases that are busy at different times, such as one per store or per customer of a SaaS product
SQL Managed Instance | a whole managed SQL Server instance in a subnet of your virtual network | the same, plus the network | existing apps that need SQL Server Agent, cross-database queries or linked servers
SQL Server on Azure VMs | a virtual machine with SQL Server installed (IaaS) | everything from the operating system up | full control, older versions, other software on the machine

With the two PaaS options, Microsoft patches the engine, takes the backups and keeps the database highly available. On a VM, the SQL IaaS Agent extension adds management features in the portal, but keeping the VM and SQL Server patched, backed up and highly available remains your job.

SQL Database introduces a concept that confuses many beginners: the logical server. When you create your first database, the portal also asks for a "server" with a name such as sql-nusa-ab12c. It is not a virtual machine; you never sign in to it or patch it. It is a management and connection boundary that:

- gives your databases a DNS name, for example sql-nusa-ab12c.database.windows.net — so the name must be globally unique;
- holds settings that apply to every database on it: firewall rules, the Microsoft Entra administrator, auditing and the connection policy;
- contains a small master database with server-level metadata.

The logical server has no price of its own; you pay per database or per elastic pool. Databases on the same server can use different tiers and sizes. A server lives in one region, and so do its databases.

Why would anyone choose a pool? Imagine forty small store databases. Each store is busy at its own opening hours and quiet the rest of the day. Sized one by one, every database needs enough capacity for its own peak, and most of that capacity sits idle. In a pool, they share capacity sized for the combined peak, which is far smaller than the sum of forty individual peaks. A pool stops paying off when the databases all peak at the same moment.

3. Paying for it: purchasing models, service tiers and serverless

Azure SQL Database offers two purchasing models. Both give you the same engine; they differ in how you size and pay.

| DTU model | vCore model
What you buy | DTUs (Database Transaction Units): a fixed blend of CPU, memory and I/O | a number of vCores on a chosen hardware generation, with storage sized separately
Service tiers | Basic, Standard, Premium | General Purpose, Business Critical, Hyperscale
Strengths | simple, predictable price for small, steady databases | flexible; serverless compute; Azure Hybrid Benefit and reservations for provisioned compute
Typical use | a small departmental app, a quick prototype | most new production workloads

You are not locked in. A database can move between tiers, and from the DTU model to the vCore model, with a scaling operation that keeps the data online and ends with a short reconnect. That makes it safe to start small and resize when real usage data arrives.

Within the vCore model, the service tier decides the architecture underneath your database:

Tier | How it works, in one line | Good for
General Purpose | stateless compute nodes in front of remote, highly durable storage | most business applications, dev/test; serverless and the free offer live here
Business Critical | several replicas kept in sync on fast local SSD storage | low-latency transactional apps that need the fastest failover; includes a readable replica for reports
Hyperscale | compute separated from a distributed layer of page servers and a log service | large or fast-growing databases, up to 128 TB, with quick scaling and restores

Next comes the compute tier. Provisioned compute reserves a fixed number of vCores, billed per hour whether you use them or not. Serverless compute, available in General Purpose and Hyperscale, scales automatically between a minimum and a maximum number of vCores and bills per second for what the database actually uses.

General Purpose serverless can also auto-pause: after a period with no connections (the auto-pause delay, 60 minutes by default and 15 minutes at minimum) the database pauses, and you pay only for storage. The next connection wakes it up. Resuming usually takes under a minute, and the first connection attempt fails with error 40613 ("database not currently available") while that happens, so applications need retry logic. Auto-pause for Hyperscale serverless was still in preview at the time of writing.

Finally, the free offer. At the time of writing (October 2026), every subscription can create up to ten free General Purpose serverless databases. Each one gets 100,000 vCore-seconds of compute, 32 GB of data and 32 GB of backup storage every month, renewed for the life of the subscription. That is about 28 hours of one busy vCore per month — plenty for development and labs. When the allowance runs out, you choose what happens: the database pauses until the next month (the default), or it keeps running and bills the extra usage. Free databases have limits: at most 4 vCores, 7 days of point-in-time restore, locally redundant backups only, and no elastic pools or failover groups. Check the current terms before you rely on them.

Tip: Auto-pause only works when nothing is connected. A query window or an object explorer left open in a tool keeps the database awake — and burns compute or free vCore-seconds. Close your tools when you finish, and set a metric alert on the free amount remaining if you use the free offer.

4. Getting in: gateway, firewall and Microsoft Entra authentication

A connection to Azure SQL Database passes several checkpoints before it can read a single row.

The gateway. The server name resolves to a regional gateway that listens on TCP port 1433. The server's connection policy decides what happens next. With Redirect, the client is told where the database is really hosted and talks to that node directly on ports 11000–11999, which lowers latency. With Proxy, every packet keeps flowing through the gateway. The Default policy uses Redirect for clients inside Azure and Proxy for clients outside.

The firewall. A new server denies every IP address. You open it with server-level IP firewall rules, which apply to all databases on the server, or with database-level rules, which you create with T-SQL and which travel with the database. Rule changes can take up to five minutes to apply. There is also a switch called Allow Azure services and resources to access this server. It creates a special 0.0.0.0 rule that admits any address inside Azure, including resources in other customers' subscriptions. For private-only access you will later use private endpoints (Lunches 25 and 28).

Warning: "Just open port 1433 to the internet" usually ends as a rule from 0.0.0.0 to 255.255.255.255, or the Allow Azure services switch turned on for convenience. Combined with a guessable SQL password, that is a classic breach. Allow specific client IP addresses only, and remove rules you no longer need.

Authentication. Getting past the firewall only brings you to the sign-in. Azure SQL supports two methods. SQL authentication uses a login and password stored in the database engine. Microsoft Entra authentication uses tokens from Microsoft Entra ID (Lunch 05). Entra brings MFA, Conditional Access, groups and — for applications — managed identities, which means no secrets in code at all.

Every server can have one Microsoft Entra admin, a user or, better, a group. Turn on Microsoft Entra-only authentication and SQL authentication stops working for the whole server, including the SQL admin login created with it. Other people get access as contained database users created from their Entra identities, for example CREATE USER [dewi@nusantararetail.co.id] FROM EXTERNAL PROVIDER;, followed by a database role such as db_datareader.

Encryption is on by default in both directions that matter: connections use TLS, and every new database is encrypted at rest with transparent data encryption (TDE) using a service-managed key.

5. Built-in backups and the tools you will use

Pak Budi's USB drive can finally retire. Azure SQL Database backs up every database automatically: a full backup every week, a differential backup every 12 or 24 hours, and a transaction log backup about every 10 minutes. Together they allow point-in-time restore (PITR) to any moment inside the retention window — 7 days by default, adjustable from 1 to 35 days (Basic tier: up to 7). A restore always creates a new database next to the original, so you can compare before you switch. Long-term retention keeps weekly, monthly or yearly full backups for up to 10 years. The first full backup starts right after a database is created and usually finishes within 30 minutes. Lunch 17 covers backup strategy in general; Lunch 28 goes deeper into Azure SQL backups and disaster recovery.

To talk to the database, you need a client tool:

Tool | Runs on | Best for | Good to know
Query editor in the Azure portal | your browser | quick queries and checks | supports Entra and SQL authentication; cannot connect to master; queries time out after 5 minutes; needs only port 443
VS Code with the MSSQL extension | Windows, macOS, Linux | everyday development | the recommended replacement for Azure Data Studio, which was retired on February 28, 2026
sqlcmd | command line, including Cloud Shell | scripts and automation | comes in two variants (ODBC-based and Go-based); Cloud Shell includes one, and the lab shows how to use it with an Entra token
SQL Server Management Studio (SSMS) | Windows | full administration | the classic tool for database administrators

Whatever the tool, the checkpoints from section 4 still apply: your client's IP address must be allowed by the firewall, and your identity must be allowed by the database. Three surprises catch almost everyone at least once:

- The portal Query editor connects from your browser's public IP address, which is usually not Cloud Shell's address, so each needs its own firewall rule.
- Cloud Shell can get a different public IP address in a new session. A rule that worked yesterday may not match today; the error message tells you which address was refused.
- Many office networks block outbound port 1433. Tools then time out instead of showing a clear error. The Query editor, which needs only port 443, is a handy way to tell a network problem from a database problem.

6. How it fits together for Nusantara Retail

Walk the orders through the decision flow. The data is relational, Dewi's code already speaks T-SQL, nobody needs the operating system, and the app uses no instance features. The answer is Azure SQL Database, a single database in the General Purpose tier:

- Development and testing use the free offer, which pauses itself when nobody is working.
- Production starts on General Purpose serverless while traffic is modest, then moves to provisioned vCores once the load is steady enough to justify paying for a fixed size. The data stays in Indonesia Central for residency; the labs use Southeast Asia for broad service availability.
- Access runs through Microsoft Entra-only authentication. The Entra admin is a group, not a person. Dewi's team gets contained database users with only the roles it needs, and the storefront app will use a managed identity (Lunch 15), so no password appears in any configuration file.
- The firewall allows only known addresses. Rizky's "open it to the internet" idea is politely declined; a private endpoint will replace public access later.
- Backups are automatic, with point-in-time restore replacing the USB drive.

And the finance team's question? The logical server itself is free. A serverless database costs compute per second while it works plus storage per GB, and nothing for compute while it is paused. The test database costs nothing while it stays within the free allowance. Use the pricing calculator for real numbers in your region, and keep the budget from Lunch 01 in place.

The other teams get answers too. Finance's old accounting package uses SQL Server Agent jobs and cross-database queries, so it is a candidate for SQL Managed Instance. The marketing team's WordPress site belongs on Azure Database for MySQL flexible server. The product catalogue, with its ever-changing attributes, is the subject of the next lunch: Azure Cosmos DB.

Pause and think: Rizky's reporting tool runs on a VM in Azure. Which is the better way to let it reach the database: turning on Allow Azure services, adding a firewall rule for the VM's public IP address, or a private endpoint? What does each option let in besides Rizky's VM?

Ready for more? Lunch 28 · Relational Databases (Advanced) (https://stefpin.github.io/azure-fundamentals-lunches/en/lunches/28-relational-databases-advanced.html) covers high availability, failover groups, backups in depth and advanced security for Azure SQL.

Field notes from Stefanus

A backup you have never restored is only a rumour. Automatic backups are the best thing about Azure SQL Database, and the easiest to take for granted. So in the first week of every new database I restore it on purpose: I pick a moment from yesterday, run a point-in-time restore next to the original, count the rows and time how long it takes. That small drill answers questions no diagram can: how long a restore of this size really takes, who has the permissions to start one, and how the application gets pointed at the restored copy, which always has a new name. I write the answers into the runbook while they are fresh. When something goes wrong at a bad hour, nobody should be reading the documentation for the first time.

Go further

- Microsoft Learn: What is Azure SQL? (https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/azure-sql/azure-sql-iaas-vs-paas-what-is-overview) — the three deployment options compared side by side, with links into each.
- Microsoft Learn: Deploy Azure SQL Database for free (https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/azure-sql/database/free-offer) — the current free-offer terms and limits; check them before you rely on the numbers above.
- Microsoft Learn: Serverless compute tier for Azure SQL Database (https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/azure-sql/database/serverless-tier-overview) — how auto-scaling, auto-pause and billing work in detail.
- Microsoft Learn training: Explore relational database services in Azure (https://learn.microsoft.com/training/modules/explore-provision-deploy-relational-database-offerings-azure/) — a short beginner module that reinforces today's choice matrix.

quiz.q: Finance's accounting package uses SQL Server Agent jobs and queries that join tables across three databases. The team wants to stop patching servers. Which Azure SQL deployment option fits best?
quiz.a: Azure SQL Managed Instance. It keeps instance-level features such as SQL Server Agent and cross-database queries, while Microsoft patches and backs it up — SQL Database lacks those features, and a VM would keep the patching work.

quiz.q: Dewi's test database is used for about an hour a day and sits idle the rest of the time. Which compute option keeps the bill lowest without changing the engine?
quiz.a: General Purpose serverless with auto-pause (or the free offer, which is serverless too). Compute is billed per second while it runs, and only storage is billed while the database is paused.

quiz.q: Rizky's reporting tool runs in Azure, so he asks you to turn on Allow Azure services and resources to access this server. What is the problem with that?
quiz.a: The switch admits connections from any Azure IP address, including other customers' resources, not just Rizky's tool. Use a rule for his specific IP address or, better, a private endpoint — and keep Entra authentication on.

quiz.q: After you enable Microsoft Entra-only authentication, an old script that signs in with the SQL admin login and password stops working. What happened, and what is the right fix?
quiz.a: Entra-only authentication disables SQL authentication for the whole server, including the SQL admin. Give the script an Entra identity (a managed identity if it runs in Azure) and a contained database user with only the roles it needs — do not switch SQL authentication back on.

quiz.q: Someone deleted half of the Orders table two hours ago. Nobody configured any backup. Can you get the rows back?
quiz.a: Yes. Azure SQL Database takes automatic backups, so you can run a point-in-time restore to a moment just before the delete. It creates a new database that you can compare and copy from; the default retention is 7 days.

takeaways: Choose a database in three steps: the data model (relational or NoSQL), then the engine (SQL Server, PostgreSQL or MySQL), then how much control you need (SQL Database → Managed Instance → VM).
A logical server is a connection and management boundary — DNS name, firewall rules, Entra admin — not a virtual machine; you pay per database or elastic pool.
The vCore model (General Purpose, Business Critical, Hyperscale) is the flexible default; serverless with auto-pause and the free offer make small and development databases close to free.
Every connection passes the gateway and the server firewall before authentication: allow specific IP addresses only, and use Microsoft Entra-only authentication so no shared passwords exist.
Backups, point-in-time restore, high availability and encryption are built in; query with the portal Query editor, VS Code with the MSSQL extension, or sqlcmd.

lab.title: Nusantara Retail's orders database
lab.text:
What you'll build

Nusantara Retail's orders move out of the SQL Server Express database next to the pantry and into Azure SQL Database. You create a logical server that accepts only Microsoft Entra sign-ins — no shared sa password exists — with yourself as the admin. You add a database, sqldb-orders, on the free offer (or on serverless compute with auto-pause if the free offer is not available to you). You open the server firewall for exactly one IP address, then create and query an Orders table from Cloud Shell with sqlcmd and from the portal Query editor. Finally, you break the firewall rule on purpose to see the error your users would get, and fix it.

Before you start

- An Azure subscription where you can create resources (see Lab 01 (https://stefpin.github.io/azure-fundamentals-lunches/en/labs/01-before-you-begin.html)). Sign in with a user account: the lab makes that account the database administrator.
- Azure Cloud Shell (Bash) — open shell.azure.com. Nothing to install: Cloud Shell already has the Azure CLI and sqlcmd.
- Get the lab files and load the shared settings and a few names you will reuse:

git clone https://github.com/stefpin/azure-fundamentals-lunches.git   # first time only
cd azure-fundamentals-lunches/labs/11-relational-databases-basic
source ../common/config.sh
RG=$(rg_name 11)
SQL_SERVER="sql-nusa-${SUFFIX}"
SQL_FQDN="${SQL_SERVER}.database.windows.net"
DB=sqldb-orders
source azsql.sh            # defines the 'azsql' helper used in Task 4

Tip: Cloud Shell ends a session after about 20 minutes without activity, and variables disappear with it. If that happens, cd back into the lab folder and run the block above again (skip the git clone).

Important: Lab resources cost money while they exist. Finish with the Clean up section, even if you stop halfway.

Choose your mode

Mode | For you if… | How
Guided | you want every step explained | follow Tasks 1–5 below
Challenge | you already know the basics | read only the Challenge brief, build it your way, then run bash verify.sh

Task 1 · Create a logical server with Microsoft Entra-only authentication

The logical server gives your database its DNS name and holds the firewall rules and the Microsoft Entra admin. With Entra-only authentication, SQL logins and passwords are switched off for the whole server, so there is no sa password to leak. You will be the admin, identified by your user principal name (UPN) and object ID.

ensure_rg "$RG" 11
MY_UPN=$(my_upn)
MY_OID=$(my_object_id)
echo "The admin will be: $MY_UPN ($MY_OID)"

az sql server create \
  --name "$SQL_SERVER" \
  --resource-group "$RG" \
  --location "$LOCATION" \
  --enable-ad-only-auth \
  --external-admin-principal-type User \
  --external-admin-name "$MY_UPN" \
  --external-admin-sid "$MY_OID" \
  --output none

Creating the server takes one to three minutes. Notice what you did not type: an admin login and password. Azure still creates an internal SQL admin with a random password, but Entra-only authentication means nobody can use it.

Tip: Prefer the portal? Home › SQL servers › + Create — pick the resource group, enter the server name and region, choose Authentication method: Use Microsoft Entra-only authentication, select Set admin and choose your own account. Then come back and continue with Task 2.

Checkpoint: both commands show your settings — azureAdOnlyAuthentication is True, and the admin is you.

az sql server ad-only-auth get --resource-group "$RG" --name "$SQL_SERVER" --output table
az sql server ad-admin list --resource-group "$RG" --server "$SQL_SERVER" \
  --query "[].{admin:login, type:administratorType, objectId:sid}" --output table

Task 2 · Create the database on the free offer (or serverless)

The free offer gives each subscription up to ten General Purpose serverless databases with a monthly allowance of compute, data and backup storage. You ask for it with --use-free-limit, and --free-limit-exhaustion-behavior AutoPause tells Azure to pause the database — never to bill you — if the allowance runs out.

az sql db create \
  --resource-group "$RG" \
  --server "$SQL_SERVER" \
  --name "$DB" \
  --edition GeneralPurpose --family Gen5 --capacity 2 \
  --compute-model Serverless \
  --use-free-limit \
  --free-limit-exhaustion-behavior AutoPause \
  --output none

Important: If the free offer fails — for example because your subscription already uses its free databases, they live in another region, or your subscription type is not eligible — create a regular serverless database with auto-pause instead. It costs a little while it runs and only storage while it is paused:

az sql db create \
  --resource-group "$RG" \
  --server "$SQL_SERVER" \
  --name "$DB" \
  --edition GeneralPurpose --family Gen5 --capacity 1 \
  --compute-model Serverless --min-capacity 0.5 --auto-pause-delay 60 \
  --backup-storage-redundancy Local \
  --output none

--capacity 1 is the maximum number of vCores, --min-capacity 0.5 the minimum while it runs, and --auto-pause-delay 60 the idle minutes before it pauses. Locally redundant backups are the cheapest option and are fine for a lab.

Tip: Prefer the portal? Home › SQL databases › + Create. On the free offer, a "Free offer applied" banner appears at the top of the page and the cost summary shows zero. Choose the server from Task 1 and keep the defaults.

Checkpoint: the database exists on serverless compute (GP_S_Gen5_…) with an auto-pause delay. freeOffer shows True if the free offer applied.

az sql db show --resource-group "$RG" --server "$SQL_SERVER" --name "$DB" \
  --query "{sku:currentServiceObjectiveName, status:status, autoPauseMinutes:autoPauseDelay, freeOffer:useFreeLimit, whenFreeUsedUp:freeLimitExhaustionBehavior}" \
  --output table

Task 3 · Open the firewall for your client IP address

A new server rejects every IP address. Add a server-level firewall rule for the public IP address that Cloud Shell uses right now. The my_public_ip helper asks a public "what is my IP" service.

MY_IP=$(my_public_ip)
echo "Cloud Shell's public IP right now: $MY_IP"

az sql server firewall-rule create \
  --resource-group "$RG" \
  --server "$SQL_SERVER" \
  --name AllowMyClientIP \
  --start-ip-address "$MY_IP" \
  --end-ip-address "$MY_IP" \
  --output none

Two things to know. First, Cloud Shell can get a different public IP address in a new session; when that happens, run these commands again — creating a rule with an existing name updates it. Second, firewall changes can take up to five minutes to apply.

Warning: Do not turn on Allow Azure services and resources to access this server to make Cloud Shell work. It would, because Cloud Shell runs in Azure — but so would every other Azure customer's resources.

Tip: Prefer the portal? SQL server › Security › Networking › Firewall rules › + Add your client IPv4 address. Look closely: that button adds your browser's IP address, not Cloud Shell's. You will need exactly that in Task 5.

Checkpoint: one rule, AllowMyClientIP, whose start and end address equal $MY_IP.

az sql server firewall-rule list --resource-group "$RG" --server "$SQL_SERVER" --output table

Task 4 · Connect with sqlcmd as yourself and create the Orders table

Cloud Shell includes the ODBC-based sqlcmd. For Microsoft Entra authentication it does not take a password: you give it an access token from Microsoft Entra ID in a small file. The azsql helper you loaded at the start does exactly that on every call — it asks the Azure CLI for a fresh token for Azure SQL, runs sqlcmd with -G (use Entra) and -P <token file>, then deletes the file.

Curious? This is what azsql runs for you

( umask 077                                                        # keep the token file private
  az account get-access-token --resource https://database.windows.net --query accessToken --output tsv \
    | tr -d '\r\n' | iconv -f ascii -t UTF-16LE > ~/.azsql-token )  # sqlcmd wants UTF-16LE, no BOM
sqlcmd -S "$SQL_FQDN" -d "$DB" -G -P ~/.azsql-token -Q "SELECT SUSER_SNAME();"
rm ~/.azsql-token                                                  # the token is valid for about an hour

First, check who you are inside the database:

azsql "$SQL_FQDN" "$DB" -W -Q "SELECT SUSER_SNAME() AS signed_in_as, DB_NAME() AS database_name;"

You should see your own UPN — no password was involved. If you get error 40613 ("is not currently available"), a paused database is waking up: wait 30–60 seconds and run the command again.

Now create the table and the sample orders. Have a look at orders.sql first: it creates dbo.Orders and inserts seven orders from different stores. The script is safe to run twice.

azsql "$SQL_FQDN" "$DB" -i orders.sql

Query the data:

azsql "$SQL_FQDN" "$DB" -W -Q "SELECT OrderId, StoreCode, CustomerName, TotalIdr, Status FROM dbo.Orders ORDER BY OrderId;"

Checkpoint: the last command lists seven orders, from JKT-01 to MKS-01. orders.sql ended with order_count = 7.

Task 5 · Query the database from the portal Query editor

The Query editor runs in your browser, so it connects from your browser's public IP address — a different client, with a different address, from Cloud Shell. It is the quickest way to check data without installing anything.

1. In the portal, open SQL databases › sqldb-orders › Query editor.
2. Choose Microsoft Entra authentication and continue as yourself.
3. If you see a firewall error that names an IP address, select the Allowlist IP … link in the error (or add the address under the server's Networking page), wait a moment, and connect again.
4. Paste this query into the editor and select Run:
  SELECT StoreCode, COUNT(*) AS orders, SUM(TotalIdr) AS revenue_idr
  FROM dbo.Orders
  GROUP BY StoreCode
  ORDER BY revenue_idr DESC;

5. Add one order from the browser, then run the query from step 4 again:
  INSERT INTO dbo.Orders (StoreCode, CustomerName, TotalIdr) VALUES ('JKT-01', N'Dewi Anggraini', 99000);

Checkpoint: the results grid shows revenue per store, and JKT-01 now has two orders. In Cloud Shell, az sql server firewall-rule list --resource-group "$RG" --server "$SQL_SERVER" --output table shows a second rule for your browser's address.

Break it and fix it

Your firewall rule is the only thing that lets Cloud Shell in. Remove it and see what your users would see.

az sql server firewall-rule delete --resource-group "$RG" --server "$SQL_SERVER" --name AllowMyClientIP
azsql "$SQL_FQDN" "$DB" -Q "SELECT COUNT(*) AS orders FROM dbo.Orders;"

Symptom: error 40615 — Cannot open server 'sql-nusa-…' requested by the login. Client with IP address '…' is not allowed to access the server. If the query still works, wait a minute or two and try again: firewall changes can take up to five minutes to apply. Notice that authentication never happened — the firewall stopped the connection first. Meanwhile, the portal Query editor keeps working. Why?

Hint: how to fix it

Recreate the rule for your current address — the error message even tells you which address was refused:

MY_IP=$(my_public_ip)
az sql server firewall-rule create --resource-group "$RG" --server "$SQL_SERVER" --name AllowMyClientIP \
  --start-ip-address "$MY_IP" --end-ip-address "$MY_IP" --output none

Wait a minute, then run the azsql query again. The Query editor kept working because your browser's IP address has its own rule: each client address is allowed (or refused) separately.

Verify your work

bash verify.sh

Every check should say PASS. If one fails, the message tells you which task to revisit. The row count is checked only where sqlcmd is installed — run verify.sh in Cloud Shell.

Clean up (do not skip!)

bash cleanup.sh

This deletes the resource group rg-lunch11-<suffix>, and with it the server, the database and the firewall rules. The lab created nothing outside the resource group. Deletion continues in the background for a few minutes.

Troubleshooting

Symptom | Likely cause | Fix
Location '…' is not accepting creation of new Windows Azure SQL Database servers for the subscription '…' at this time. | Your subscription cannot create SQL servers in that region right now | Run bash cleanup.sh and wait until az group list --tag lunch=11 --output table is empty (the resource group was already created in the old region), then export LOCATION=<another region>, source ../common/config.sh, and start again from Task 1
az sql server create says the server name already exists | Server names are global DNS names; yours is already taken (perhaps by an old lab run) | Delete the old server, or set a new SUFFIX before sourcing config.sh
az sql db create with --use-free-limit fails | No free database left in your subscription, free databases in another region, or a subscription type that is not eligible | Use the serverless command in the Task 2 box
Error 40615: Client with IP address '…' is not allowed to access the server | No firewall rule matches your current IP — Cloud Shell's IP may have changed | Re-run the Task 3 commands, wait up to five minutes, retry
Error 40613: Database 'sqldb-orders' on server '…' is not currently available | The serverless database is paused and is resuming | Wait 30–60 seconds and run the command again
Login failed for user '<token-identified principal>' | You are signed in to Azure as a different account from the server's Entra admin | Run az account show --query user.name; sign in as the admin or add yourself as a database user
Could not get a Microsoft Entra access token for Azure SQL | Your Cloud Shell or CLI session has expired | Run az login, then try again
sqlcmd: command not found or a login timeout from your own PC | You are not in Cloud Shell, or your network blocks outbound port 1433 | Use Cloud Shell, or the portal Query editor (port 443 only)

Stretch goals

- Give a second account in your own tenant read-only access: in the Query editor run CREATE USER [user@yourtenant.onmicrosoft.com] FROM EXTERNAL PROVIDER; and ALTER ROLE db_datareader ADD MEMBER [user@yourtenant.onmicrosoft.com];, then sign in as that user in a private browser window and try an INSERT.
- Connect from VS Code with the MSSQL extension on your own PC, using Microsoft Entra ID authentication. You will need a firewall rule for your PC's address too.
- If you used the serverless fallback, set --auto-pause-delay 15 with az sql db update, close every tool, and check az sql db show ... --query status after about 20 minutes: it should say Paused.
- On the free offer, open the database's Overview › Free monthly vCore amount metric and create an alert for when fewer than 10,000 vCore-seconds remain.

Challenge brief

Build the following, any way you like (portal, CLI, Bicep):

1. A resource group rg-lunch11-<suffix> created with ensure_rg (or tagged course=azure-fundamentals-lunches and lunch=11) in your lab region.
2. A logical server sql-nusa-<suffix> with Microsoft Entra-only authentication enabled and your own account as the Microsoft Entra admin.
3. A database sqldb-orders on General Purpose serverless compute with auto-pause enabled — on the free offer if your subscription allows it.
4. A server-level firewall rule that allows your current Cloud Shell IP address, and no rule that allows all Azure services or the whole internet.
5. A table dbo.Orders with at least one order in it (orders.sql adds seven).

Then run bash verify.sh. Stuck? Peek at solution.sh or switch to Guided mode.
